validator: draft 1 passed with no hard problems, no soft problems and no warnings. The faults below are the critic's.
keep: The idea is named in two plain sentences up front: each mark means one thing, so you read a symbol mark by mark and can name one you have never seen. Hydraulic and air share the marks.

Thirteen screens: the recall opener (1, Heat and fluids lesson 5's jack, the same 100 N, 10 cm² and 200 cm², typed, 'Still there.'), then SHOW 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 alternating with DO 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, ending with two mixed puzzles (12, 13).

Every lesson 4 misconception in the brief has a DO screen with its own hint: pump and motor swapped (3, 12 and 13's slips), the symbol read as the build or the port layout (9, after the cutaway on 8), a turned symbol read as a new part (11, two filters, and 13's slip 1), and not knowing the symbols (the matching shelf on 10, and 12).

The cause is drawn: one switch flips one mark and the name changes at once, so he sees that each mark carries one meaning. The cutaway switch changes the build while the symbol stays put, which shows Bosch's rule rather than telling it.
The three counts (1, 5, 13) are typed whole numbers; each wrong figure is a slip with the hint that names its mistake. The rest choose between named parts or sets of marks, so they stay as options.

Only two sources carry this idea and both are cited on the words their quotes support: the pump and motor triangle on DOE's point-and-tail line, and 'not how it is built' on Bosch. Valves, the tank's line rule and cylinder sizing are left to lessons 5 and 6 and to Hydraulics and pneumatics.
Safety comes first in practice: a symbol does not show stored pressure, and an accumulator can hold it with the pump stopped.
The analogy is from his trade, the slanted arrow on a variable resistor and the arrows on an LED, different from lessons 1 to 3, and it says where it breaks.
fix: Talks against its own rule: explain and the tray say 'a box is a cylinder, or one position of a valve', one mark with two meanings in a lesson whose claim is that each mark means one thing. Split it: a square is one valve position (lesson 5 reads it), and a long box with a piston and rod is a cylinder.

Causal step skipped: explain says a symbol shows function, not build, but never why that is enough. Add that a circuit is traced by what each part does to the flow, so the build would only crowd the sheet.
Loose count: 'Three marks, each with two choices, name eight different machines' reads as if the circle were one of the three. Say three marks on the circle, each one of two ways.
Analogy break overstated: 'a plain circle is a pump or a motor' is not true of a plain circle; it is the circle with a triangle. Say that.

SHOW screen 10 names the diamond, filter, cylinder and tank but drags six symbols. Keep it to three sentences, and let the read name all six; no change to the count, but name the accumulator's job in whatAmILookingAt's cards so the drag has words to match.

Unsourced general claim: 'Most symbols mean the same however they are turned' has no quote in this course's research. It is textbook-standard and hedged with 'most'; keep it unfootnoted and plain, and keep the tank's exception out rather than state an unquoted rule.
